title: Hyrum's Law Violation (Leaking Implementation Invariants)
pattern: Exposing raw, implementation-specific structures (like a standard `HashMap` or a private sorting order) directly in a public API, allowing callers to depend on undocumented behavioral side-effects (like the exact hashing or iteration order).
why_bad: The library's internal behavior becomes locked. Any attempt to optimize performance (e.g., swapping `HashMap` for an index map or updating a compiler version that alters the hashing seed) breaks downstream callers who implicitly depended on the undocumented behavioral order.
detection: Public fields or API return signatures that expose raw collection types (`HashMap`, `HashSet`) rather than encapsulated opaque iterators or wrapper types.
counterexample: Internal-only structures or simple, raw data-transfer structs (DTOs) whose sole purpose is to act as dumb data holders.
fix: Encapsulate the collection. Expose custom, stable accessor methods (like `pub fn get_user(&self, id: &str) -> Option<&User>`) and hide the underlying storage collection behind a private visibility modifier.
source: Titus Winters, Tom Manshreck, Hyrum Wright, *Software Engineering at Google* (2020), Chapter 1 ("Time and Change: Hyrum's Law"), p. 7.
